lesson.title: Knowing When to Stop: Contact Inhibition
lesson.summary: Contact inhibition is the normal behavior in which cells stop dividing once they are surrounded by neighboring cells, and its loss is one of the clearest hallmarks of a cancer cell in culture.
lesson.body:
Cell division does not only respond to internal checkpoints, DNA damage sensors, and cyclin levels. It also responds to information from a cell's surroundings, including, quite literally, whether the cell is touching its neighbors. Normal cells grown in a laboratory dish will divide and spread across the available surface, but once they make contact with neighboring cells on all sides and form a complete, single layer sheet, they stop dividing. This phenomenon is called contact inhibition, and it is a normal, healthy feature of how most cells regulate their own growth.

Contact inhibition works through cell signaling. Proteins on the surface of one cell, including adhesion molecules that physically link neighboring cells together, generate signals when a cell becomes surrounded by others, and those signals feed into the same kind of signal transduction pathways covered generally in cell signaling, ultimately restraining progression through the G1 checkpoint. One well documented signaling network involved in this process is called the Hippo pathway, which becomes active as cell density increases and restrains the activity of growth promoting transcription factors, effectively telling a crowded cell that there is no more room to grow. In short, a cell that is surrounded receives less encouragement to divide, and more discouragement, than a cell with open space around it.

Contact inhibition is one of the clearest ways to see the difference between a normal cell and a cancer cell in the laboratory. Normal cells stop dividing at confluence and form a flat, orderly monolayer. Cancer cells, having lost tumor suppressor function or gained oncogene activity as covered in the cancer biology chapter, ignore these contact signals entirely. They keep dividing after making contact with their neighbors, piling up on top of one another in disorganized clumps called foci instead of stopping at a single layer. This behavior is distinctive enough that scientists use it as a direct laboratory test, a focus formation assay, to identify whether a gene or mutation is capable of transforming a normal cell into a cancer like one.

Inside the body, the loss of contact inhibition has consequences well beyond a messy cell culture dish. A normal tissue relies on cells respecting their neighbors' boundaries to maintain organized structure, whether in skin, the lining of the gut, or any other tissue built from tightly packed cells. A tumor cell that ignores contact signals keeps growing past the point where a normal cell would stop, contributing directly to the uncontrolled mass of a tumor and, eventually, to its ability to push into and invade surrounding healthy tissue.
